title: One Missing Protein, A Cortex Built Wrong

scenes.tts: A mouse reels from side to side as it walks. Its cerebellum is small. The layers of its cerebral cortex are disorganized, and roughly in reverse order. Why would a mouse that cannot walk straight have a cortex built in the wrong order? One missing protein explains both.
scenes.visual: A wobbling walk, a small cerebellum, and two cortex stacks (normal, then reversed) with a question mark; a yellow chip for one missing protein points to both.
scenes.narration: A mouse reels from side to side as it walks. Its cerebellum is small. The layers of its cerebral cortex are disorganized, and roughly in reverse order. Why would a mouse that cannot walk straight have a cortex built in the wrong order? One missing protein explains both.

scenes.tts: Neurons leave the ventricular zone and climb toward the surface. The first ones form a thin sheet just under it. The next ones move into the middle of that sheet and split it in two. The upper part, the marginal zone, holds Cajal-Retzius cells. Each new wave climbs past the last, so early-born neurons end up deep and late-born neurons end up superficial.
scenes.visual: A cortex slab: orange neurons climb into a thin sheet, blue neurons enter and split it, the top half becomes yellow Cajal-Retzius cells, then green neurons climb past the blue ones.
scenes.narration: Neurons leave the ventricular zone and climb toward the surface. The first ones form a thin sheet just under it. The next ones move into the middle of that sheet and split it in two. The upper part, the marginal zone, holds Cajal-Retzius cells. Each new wave climbs past the last, so early-born neurons end up deep and late-born neurons end up superficial.

scenes.tts: Was reeler making the wrong neurons, or putting the right ones in the wrong place? Birthdating showed the same classes of neurons, born on the same schedule as in normal mice. But early-born neurons tended to sit near the surface, and late-born neurons deep. The first sheet fails to split, and each later wave stops beneath the neurons already there. The neurons are made, but they cannot get past their elders.
scenes.visual: Normal slab beside a reeler slab; the three waves rise in reeler and stack in reverse order under the first sheet; red stop bars block each wave.

scenes.tts: Cajal-Retzius cells make a very large secreted protein called Reelin. It is made at the top of the cortex, the very place where each new wave should stop. Reelin binds two lipoprotein receptors, Apo E R two and V L D L R. Inside the neuron, the kinases Fyn and Sark then add a phosphate to an adaptor called Dab one.
scenes.visual: A yellow cell releases Reelin onto two teal receptors in the neuron surface; Dab1 hangs from their tails; the kinases arrive and a phosphate badge lands on Dab1.
scenes.caption: Cajal-Retzius cells make a very large secreted protein called Reelin. It is made at the top of the cortex, the very place where each new wave should stop. Reelin binds two lipoprotein receptors, ApoER2 and VLDLR. Inside the neuron, the kinases Fyn and Src then add a phosphate to an adaptor called Dab1.

Reelin binds two lipoprotein receptors, ApoER2 and VLDLR. Inside the neuron, the kinases Fyn and Src then add a phosphate to an adaptor called Dab1.

scenes.tts: In a relay race, remove any runner and the baton never arrives. Reeler mice lack Reelin. Mice without Dab one look the same. So do mice without both receptors. Matching mutants give no order, but biochemistry did: brains without Reelin held more Dab one and less phosphorylated Dab one.
scenes.visual: The Reelin chain as runners with a baton; three runners are removed in turn and the cortex result turns reeler-like each time; then bars show more Dab1 and less phosphorylated Dab1 without Reelin.

scenes.tts: Reelin is needed. But what does it tell a neuron? Perhaps stop here, or let go of the glial fiber, or come toward me. The experiments point different ways, so the question is open. A missing signal shows only that it is needed, not what it says.
scenes.visual: Three small panels at the Reelin zone: a neuron stops, a neuron lets go of its fiber, a neuron turns toward a yellow spot; question marks; the rule.
